title: Describing things
job: Size, colour, quality — agreement at length
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: un gran + N   /   un + N + grande

rules.text: An adjective in -o has four shapes and one in -e or a consonant has two: negro · negra · negros · negras, but azul · azules and grande · grandes. The second kind never marks gender at all.
"-o is masculine, -a is feminine" is about nouns, not agreement, and it is false anyway: el día, la mano, el problema. Learn every noun with its article and let the adjective follow the noun.
grande shortens to gran in front of any singular noun, and the position changes the meaning: un gran libro is a great book, un libro grande is a big one.
muy modifies an adjective and mucho modifies a verb: muy caro, but me gusta mucho. Me gusta muy and es mucho caro are both wrong, and both are word-for-word English.
The adjective normally FOLLOWS the noun: una casa nueva, un libro negro. English puts it first and never inflects it, so both halves are new.
ser describes what a thing IS LIKE and estar reports the state it is in: el libro es nuevo, la sopa está fría. It is the same split M2 drew for people.

words.note: Ends in a consonant, so it never marks gender: la puerta azul, el libro azul. Only number moves it, and then it adds -es.

sentences.trap: No feminine to write. A learner who has just met negro/negra will look for azula, and there is no such word.
sentences.sound: a-SUL, stressed on the last syllable. In most of Spain the z of azul is still an s here, because it is spelled with a z only in azul's cousins.

variations.changed: a masculine thing, and the adjective does not move
another feminine noun, same one shape
the adjective after the noun rather than after the verb

mistake.why: azul has no feminine. An adjective ending in a consonant takes one shape for both genders.

sentences.usage: Neutral description of a thing. The commonest kind of sentence there is.
sentences.mnemonic: Consonant endings do not bend for gender — only for number.

words.note: A consonant-ending adjective takes -es in the plural, not -s. The row for azul is S01's.

sentences.trap: Three words change at once — las, son, azules — and English changes only the noun. Every plural in Spanish moves everything that agrees with it.
sentences.sound: a-SU-les. The stress stays on the same syllable as in azul, so the word grows to the right.

variations.changed: masculine plural — and still one shape for the adjective
another feminine plural
no in front of the verb

mistake.why: A word ending in a consonant adds -es: azules. Bare -s only goes on a word that already ends in a vowel.

sentences.usage: Neutral. The plural is where Spanish agreement is most visible and English's least.

words.note: Ends in -e, so one shape for both genders: un libro grande, una casa grande. The plural is grandes.

sentences.trap: The adjective goes AFTER the noun. una grande casa is the English order and it is not Spanish — except when it means something else, which is S04.
sentences.sound: GRAN-de. The d between vowels is soft, closer to the th of "this".

variations.changed: masculine, and the adjective stays the same
plural, and grande adds -s because it ends in a vowel
the adjective moved behind the verb, with muy in front

mistake.why: After the noun for size: una casa grande. Before the noun it becomes gran and means something else entirely.

sentences.usage: Neutral. grande is the everyday word for big of almost anything.
sentences.mnemonic: Behind the noun it measures; in front of it, it praises.

words.note: grande with its ending cut off, and it only happens in front of a singular noun. It no longer means big: un gran libro is a great book. The row for grande is S03's.

sentences.trap: The same word, two positions, two meanings. English uses two different words — big and great — and Spanish moves one.
sentences.sound: GRAN, one syllable, and the n is fully said before the next word.

variations.changed: masculine, and gran does not change for it
another feminine noun in the same frame
gran about a person, which is where it is commonest

mistake.display: Es una gran casa, muy gran.
mistake.why: gran only stands in front of a noun. On its own, after the verb, it is grande: es muy grande.

sentences.usage: Praise rather than measurement. Un gran amigo is warm; un amigo grande is a tall one.
sentences.mnemonic: Cut the ending, change the meaning.

words.note: Four shapes, like rojo in M3 of the level below: el libro negro, la mesa negra, los libros negros.

sentences.trap: The ending tracks the noun, not the thing's colour or the speaker. la mesa negra is the same black as el libro negro.
sentences.sound: NE-gro. One tapped r, and the g is hard as in "go".

variations.changed: feminine, so the adjective ends in -a
masculine plural, everything moves together
feminine plural, the fourth cell

mistake.why: The adjective agrees with the noun it describes: negra. Nothing about the speaker enters into it.

sentences.usage: Neutral. The four-cell grid is easiest to see on a colour, which is why the module drills one.
sentences.mnemonic: Four cells, and the noun picks which.

words.note: Four shapes. It is the adjective; M9's mal is the adverb — está mal is "it's going badly", es malo is "it is a bad thing".

sentences.trap: malo and mal are not the same word. One describes a thing, the other describes how something is going.
sentences.sound: MA-lo, with a clear forward l — never the dark l English puts at the end of "pal".

variations.changed: feminine, and the adjective follows
the adjective after the noun instead of after the verb
plural throughout

mistake.why: mal never describes a thing. The adjective is malo, and it agrees.

sentences.usage: Understatement. No es malo is warmer praise in Spanish than "it's not bad" usually is in English.
sentences.mnemonic: malo describes the bread; mal describes the day.

words.note: Four shapes. After the noun it means newly made; in front of it, un nuevo libro, it means another one — the same shift gran makes.

sentences.trap: un libro nuevo is a book that is new. un nuevo libro is another book by the same author. Position again.
sentences.sound: NWE-vo — the ue is one gliding sound, and the v is said with both lips, not the teeth.

variations.changed: feminine noun, feminine adjective
plural, and the article disappears with son
after the verb, describing rather than naming

mistake.why: That is grammatical and means "another book". For a book that is new, put nuevo after it.

sentences.usage: Neutral. The pre-noun reading is common in speech, so the position is worth getting right early.
sentences.mnemonic: Behind the noun it is fresh; in front of it, it is next.

sentences.display: La casa es vieja y pequeña.
sentences.cue: The house is old and small.
sentences.literal: The house is old and small.

words.note: Old of a THING. About a person Spanish says mayor (M2) — viejo about someone's age is blunt at best.
The opposite of grande, and unlike grande it has all four shapes. The ñ is its own letter and its own sound.

sentences.trap: Two adjectives joined by y, and BOTH agree. English inflects neither and Spanish inflects every one.
sentences.sound: pe-KE-ña. The ñ is the ny of "canyon", one sound and not two.

variations.display: El libro es viejo y pequeño.
variations.cue: The book is old and small.
variations.changed: masculine, and both adjectives move
feminine plural, one adjective

variations.display: Es una casa pequeña pero nueva.
variations.cue: It's a small but new house.
variations.changed: pero sets the two descriptions against each other

mistake.display: La casa es vieja y pequeño.
mistake.why: Both adjectives describe la casa, so both are feminine: vieja y pequeña. Agreement does not stop at the first one.

sentences.usage: Neutral about things. About a person, swap vieja for mayor.
sentences.mnemonic: Every adjective in the sentence answers to the same noun.

sentences.display: Me gusta mucho, pero es muy caro.
sentences.cue: I like it a lot, but it's very expensive.
sentences.literal: To-me pleases much, but is very expensive.

words.note: Modifies the VERB and never an adjective: me gusta mucho. In front of a noun it counts it and then it agrees — muchas gracias, from M1.
Modifies an ADJECTIVE and never a verb: muy caro, muy grande. It never changes shape.

sentences.trap: English "very" and "a lot" are almost interchangeable and Spanish's are not. muy goes with adjectives, mucho with verbs, and neither ever swaps.
sentences.sound: MU-cho with the ch of "church"; MWI, one syllable, for muy.

variations.changed: the thing liked named at the end

variations.display: Es muy caro, pero me gusta.
variations.cue: It's very expensive, but I like it.
variations.changed: the halves swapped around pero
the negative, with muy untouched

mistake.why: muy cannot stand with a verb: me gusta mucho. And es mucho caro is the same error the other way round.

sentences.usage: The shape of half the opinions anyone gives about a thing they are looking at.
sentences.mnemonic: muy leans on an adjective, mucho leans on a verb.

words.note: Four cells in principle, and this course writes three: the masculine singular is spelled like M10's bueno, the word that opens a sentence with "well, …". Say es estupendo or está muy bien instead.

sentences.trap: The one adjective in this module you cannot write in every cell. It is a spelling collision, not a grammar rule, and it is worth knowing about.
sentences.sound: BWE-nas — the ue glides exactly as it does in puedo and nuevo.

variations.changed: feminine singular, the cell this module teaches first
masculine plural, which is safe to write
in front of the noun, where buena often goes

mistake.why: manzanas is feminine, so the adjective is buenas. The plural does not make everything masculine.

sentences.usage: Everyday approval. In front of a noun it is warmer; after it, more of a judgement.
sentences.mnemonic: Three cells you write, one you say another way.
